w: Dr. Geisinger opens this session with a blunt premise: treat every patient identically regardless of risk, and you are setting yourself up to fail, because periodontitis is not purely an infectious disease — it is an immuno-inflammatory one, shaped by patient-level, site-level, and environmental risk factors that drive how fast (or whether) disease progresses. "One size does not fit all" is the organizing idea for the whole lecture, and the practical question it keeps circling back to is: given everything you know about a patient, how do you turn that into an actual recall interval, an actual treatment threshold, and an actual conversation? The scale of the problem, and who is actually looking Periodontitis affects roughly 42.5% of US adults over 30 (about 64.7 million people), rising to 70.1% of adults 65 and older; it is more common in men (56.4%) than women (38.4%), and more common among current smokers (64.2%), people below the federal poverty line (65.4%), and people without a high school diploma (66.9%). The harder number to sit with is that 72% of patients ultimately diagnosed with periodontitis first walked in the door saying "I'm here for my routine cleaning" — at initial diagnosis, most patients have no idea anything is wrong. Disease doesn't hurt, bleeding on brushing gets normalized as ordinary, and no one has ever measured or explained it to them. That means the clinician is very often the first and only source of that diagnosis. Procedure-code data makes the mismatch concrete. Dentistry bills procedures, not diagnoses, and a prophylaxis (D1110) is by definition a preventive code for patients with no periodontal disease or history of it. If disease prevalence rises with age, the share of cleanings billed as prophylaxis should fall with age — instead it rises: 72.3% of cleanings are D1110 in patients 19–34, 87.5% in patients 35–49, and 95.4% in patients 50–64. That trend runs directly opposite to what the epidemiology predicts, which is the lecture's case for under-diagnosis (or under-escalation) becoming more common, not less, as patients age. P4 (P5) medicine vs. Hippocratic medicine Hippocratic medicine's first principle is "do no harm," and in practice that tends toward reactive care — treating disease once it presents rather than estimating who is headed toward it. P4 medicine — personalized, preventive, predictive, participatory — reframes care as prediction plus partnership: estimate risk, personalize that estimate to the individual patient's own risk markers, and make the patient an active participant in their own care algorithm rather than a passive recipient of instructions. Applied to periodontics specifically, the lecture calls this P5 care: personalized, preventive, predictive, participatory, periodontal. Why is estimating risk hard in the first place? Partly a data problem — "you get out what you put in." A bitewing that misses the anterior teeth can hide the worst sites in the mouth; an annual panoramic-plus-bitewing routine may simply never image the area that matters. In a UAB retrospective analysis of treated periodontal-maintenance patients, over 40% of the data had to be discarded because bleeding on probing had never actually been recorded — and if inflammation isn't charted, there is no way to size the inflammatory burden a patient is carrying. A full risk workup, practically Risk assessment is built from a patient interview (medical history, lifestyle, systemic factors), a comprehensive clinical exam (probing depths, clinical attachment levels, plaque, bleeding on probing, suppuration, furcation involvement, mobility, fremitus), diagnostic radiographs assessing alveolar bone levels, a decision about whether systemic factors need a medical consult (HbA1c for a diabetic patient, INR for a patient on anticoagulants), and a lifestyle review (tobacco, alcohol, stress). The American Academy of Periodontology recommends a comprehensive periodontal evaluation at least annually for adults, more often for higher-risk patients — and screening for disease at every patient touch, not just at a scheduled comprehensive exam. Why now? — and what a 3 mm pocket means twice The hardest question Dr. Geisinger says she gets from patients is "why now?" — someone who has kept every six-month cleaning appointment and is suddenly told they have 8 mm pockets. Those pockets did not appear overnight; the honest answer is usually some mix of failure to diagnose, failure to treat, or a kind of "good enough" treatment that never actually addressed subgingival disease — repeated supragingival-only cleanings on a patient who actually needs active periodontal therapy, a pattern the lecture calls P.E.R.I.O.D. disease: Partially Effective, Redundant Instrumentation, Overlooking Disease. Supragingival-only scaling in a periodontitis patient improves plaque scores but does not reduce probing depth or gain attachment, increases gingival bleeding and the frequency of pockets ≥4 mm, and shifts the subgingival flora toward more anaerobic, more pathogenic species (notably P. gingivalis) — something is not always better than nothing. This is also where a 3 mm probing depth means two different things. A treated periodontitis patient in maintenance has a long junctional epithelial attachment rather than a healthy connective-tissue attachment with a short junctional epithelium — that long junctional epithelium is inherently more prone to breaking down under inflammation. So a periodontally-treated patient with every site reading 3 mm is not a candidate for a plain prophylaxis the way a periodontally-naive patient with the same numbers would be; the periodontal maintenance code and protocol still apply, because the tissue itself is structurally different even once probing depths look normal. The inflammatory burden, and why it isn't "just" a mouth problem One way the lecture makes inflammatory burden concrete is the periodontal inflamed surface area (PISA): the total area of pocket epithelium facing active inflammation. A periodontally healthy patient averages a PISA around 34 mm² — roughly a small paper cut. A patient with even mild-to-moderate (Stage 1–2) periodontitis averages a PISA around 2,309 mm² — comparable to a wound the size of cellulitis with early Ludwig's angina. That gap is the argument for why periodontal disease reads as a systemic inflammatory burden, not a localized nuisance: periodontitis has documented links to over 50 systemic conditions, and a few of the better-studied connections carry real numbers — periodontitis increased the odds of dying after COVID-19 roughly nine-fold and of hospitalization roughly five-fold in one comparison; in a COPD trial, patients who received actual subgingival therapy (versus supragingival-only or no treatment) saw roughly double the reduction in COPD exacerbations; and in a diabetes trial, patients receiving intensive periodontal therapy (whole-mouth subgingival scaling, surgery where needed, 3-month maintenance) saw HbA1c fall from 8.1% to 7.8% over 12 months, while a supragingival-only control group saw HbA1c rise from 8.1% to 8.3% and recorded three deaths as adverse events during the study period. Measuring risk with a tool instead of a gut feeling Objective risk-scoring tools improve the accuracy of risk estimation over intuition alone. The lecture names several: UniFe (Trombelli et al.) scores five inputs — smoking (cigarettes/day), diabetic status (HbA1c), number of pockets ≥5 mm, bleeding-on-probing percentage, and bone-loss-to-age ratio — each 0–4, summed into a 5-tier risk score from low to high. The Periodontal Risk Assessment (PRA), from Lang and Tonetti, and PreViser/PAT (Page et al.) work on a similar principle of combining clinical, radiographic, and behavioral inputs into a single risk tier, and the lecture reports fairly good agreement between UniFe and PreViser scores when compared head-to-head on the same patients. Newer AI-assisted tools — Pearl AI and Overjet were both named — are emerging in the same space. None of these tools escapes the "garbage in, garbage out" problem: they are only as good as the clinical data fed into them. Turning a risk tier into an actual recall plan Once a patient is sorted into low, moderate, or high risk, that tier should drive concrete, different follow-up: Low risk — comprehensive periodontal exam every 6–12 months, radiographs every 12–24 months, professional biofilm/calculus removal every 6 months, standard home care (twice-daily brushing, once-daily interdental cleaning), nutrition counseling, tobacco-use prevention. Moderate risk — comprehensive exam every 6–12 months plus an oral exam/periodontal screening every 6 months, radiographs every 6–12 months, ongoing systemic-health monitoring, biofilm/calculus removal and local subgingival debridement every 4–6 months, management of plaque-retentive factors, consideration of adjunctive local antimicrobials, surgical care to arrest disease or repair defects if needed, tobacco cessation counseling, oral hygiene adjuncts (water/air flosser, adjunctive rinses or probiotics), and ongoing compliance assessment. High risk — comprehensive exam every 6–12 months plus screening every 3 months, radiographs every 6 months, close systemic monitoring with medical consults as needed, biofilm/calculus removal and subgingival debridement every 2–4 months, consideration of systemic or local adjunctive antimicrobials, surgical treatment likely necessary, and the same home-care/cessation/adjunct/compliance package as moderate risk, just monitored more tightly. Why maintenance intervals are what they are Tooth loss occurs about twice as often in treated-but-non-maintained patients versus treated-and-maintained patients, and more frequent maintenance visits correlate with fewer teeth lost over time — yet patient compliance with maintenance runs only about 30–40%. The standard 3-month interval isn't arbitrary: pathogenic subgingival species begin re-establishing within 4–8 weeks of treatment, and by 9–11 weeks the subgingival microbiome can repopulate close to pre-treatment levels — a 3-month recall sits inside that window. Patients undergoing active orthodontic tooth movement are seen more often still (roughly every 4–6 weeks), both because that's when appliances are adjusted and because inflammation during active tooth movement can uncouple bone formation from bone resorption, risking real bone loss if biofilm isn't controlled tightly during that period. Regularity of maintenance, not just total quantity of visits, is what predicts tooth-loss risk, and that effect is larger for Stage 3/4 and Grade C patients — a patient at that severity who skips more than a year of maintenance across a 5-year window has roughly 2.5x the odds of losing a tooth to periodontitis compared to one who stays regular. Communicating risk so patients actually act on it The number one reason patients decline a periodontal treatment plan is that they don't trust their dental provider — and the most trusted person in the office, by a wide margin, is the dental hygienist, not the dentist, which is the argument for a consistent message across the whole team rather than just the doctor. 62% of patients delay treatment, switch providers, seek a second opinion, or refuse care outright because they disagree with or distrust a diagnosis. Cost is rarely the real barrier: patients report they would pay an average of $633.63 per tooth to avoid losing it, and cost only becomes an objection when patients feel rushed, unable to ask questions, sense disagreement within the dental team, or aren't offered options for managing cost — in other words, when they don't yet feel that the provider genuinely cares about them specifically. A staging-and-grading diagnosis ("Stage 2 Grade B periodontitis") gives a shared, precise vocabulary for that conversation with both patients and colleagues, and the lecture models moving a patient from prophylaxis to active therapy as a four-part conversation: name what's actually been monitored and what it shows (problem), explain plainly what subgingival colonization means once probing depths exceed what home care alone can reach — roughly 1.5–2 mm — (consequence), and lay out the "prescribed" (not just "proposed") treatment plan and its benefits against the cost of doing nothing (solution). The strongest predictors of a good long-term outcome tie back to the same list this whole session is built around: oral hygiene, maintenance compliance, bleeding on probing, residual pocket depth after treatment, occlusion, bone-loss-to-age ratio, systemic/genetic factors, and cigarette smoking. In class: the three prognosis systems, compared The in-person session (a Slido review, which Dr. Geisinger said "might inform the midterm") was about telling the three prognosis systems apart by what each one is based on, not by memorizing lists. McGuire & Nunn sorts teeth by whether they can be maintained, meaning kept in the mouth. Most of the class guessed "disease progression" and was wrong. Its order is good → fair → poor → questionable → hopeless, and the classic mistake is swapping poor and questionable. Poor teeth (attachment loss, Class II furcation, mobility) can be kept with significant effort. A questionable tooth is one we genuinely question keeping, and it does not stay there: it gets worse and becomes hopeless, or it improves and moves up to poor. How accurate is it? All of the poll statements were true. It is right about 80% of the time overall (81% at 8 years). Once the good teeth are taken out of the analysis, it drops to about 50%, a coin flip. On average, teeth do better than predicted, and even hopeless teeth in well-maintained patients are often kept much longer than expected. The exceptions are smokers and patients with very poor hygiene, and even very poor hygiene tracks the prediction if those patients keep up with maintenance. Most teeth leave the mouth because a dentist extracts them, not because they exfoliate (unlike implants). McGuire & Nunn can be given per tooth or for the whole dentition, and as a diagnostic prognosis (what happens if the patient takes no treatment) or a therapeutic prognosis (how the recommended treatment changes the outcome). The therapeutic version is a good way to show a patient what treatment buys them. Kwok & Caton asks whether periodontal stability (arrested attachment loss) can be achieved with treatment: likely, don't know, or unlikely. That is why questionable sits in its middle, and why it can only ever be therapeutic. It is the better choice for a medically complex patient, because smoking or vaping cessation and referral to get an A1c under control become part of the treatment it is judging. Miller & McEntire was studied only on molars. It is quantitative (A1c, smoking and other factors get numbers), and because it was built from patients who received 30 years of treatment and maintenance, it is therapeutic too. Smoking is its biggest single risk factor: about 296% more likely to lose those molars. The one-line summary: only McGuire & Nunn can be diagnostic; all three can be therapeutic. In class: three cases, all Stage 3 A 78-year-old (ASA II, statin plus baby aspirin, #17 lost to an endodontic perforation) had mostly horizontal bone loss of about 30%, interdental CAL ≥5 mm at the worst site, and a Class II furcation. That makes her generalized Stage 3, Grade B, and her missing teeth were lost to caries, not periodontitis. Confirm the charting first: was lingual recession charted? Her Kwok & Caton prognosis was questionable, because horizontal loss and furcations are hard to regenerate. The plan was a 3-month maintenance interval (subgingival repopulation takes about 9-11 weeks, and a periodontitis patient stays higher-risk even once healthy), occlusal adjustment for secondary occlusal trauma, and attention to the recession. The Periodontal Risk Assessment (PRA), a spider-web plot of BOP, sites ≥5 mm, missing teeth, % bone loss and smoking, said to keep current measures. A 13-year-old with little plaque or inflammation had 8-11 mm pockets on first molars and #14 in a molar-incisor pattern: localized Stage 3, Grade C. Deep, narrow vertical defects respond to regeneration (bone graft, membrane, maybe a biologic) with roughly 70-75% fill, and young patients heal better. So her therapeutic McGuire & Nunn prognosis is good to fair overall, with the involved teeth fair, while her diagnostic prognosis would be poor to questionable. Regenerating a stage-defining vertical defect or furcation is the only way to move a patient back from Stage 3. About 70% of these circumpubertal patients have a neutrophil chemotactic deficiency, which is why the first teeth to erupt are hit hardest. About 70% of those whose disease generalizes use nicotine. She needs lifelong, closer maintenance and anti-nicotine counseling. A 75-year-old former smoker with BOP at about 80% of sites, 7-9 mm pockets and both vertical and horizontal defects is Stage 3, Grade C. Her overall diagnostic McGuire & Nunn prognosis is poor, even though individual teeth range from good to hopeless, which is why per-tooth prognoses are useful. With compliance and resective or regenerative care, her therapeutic prognosis improves to fair. If she later develops diabetes (A1c 8.8%), her grade can't rise past C, but her PRA footprint grows sharply. That is the point of keeping prognosis and risk tools separate from stage and grade: they capture differences the diagnosis cannot. The closing numbers: about 10% of people resist periodontitis regardless of hygiene, 10-15% are at risk for severe destructive disease, and 20-25% don't respond to standard therapy. Outcomes depend on things patients control (hygiene, attending maintenance), clinical findings (BOP, residual pockets, occlusal trauma, bone loss over age), and systemic, genetic and nicotine factors.
